title: Is fairness built into us? The monkey and the cucumber
examples: What happened in the monkey cucumber experiment?

explain.say: Have you ever shouted "That is not fair!" when someone else got a bigger slice? It turns out monkeys feel that too! Look at the board. It shows a famous experiment with capuchin monkeys, two ways side by side.

explain.say: See the left side, same reward? Two monkeys sit side by side. Each hands a small rock to a scientist and gets a piece of cucumber back. Both are calm and keep trading happily. So cucumber is a perfectly good reward. Would you be happy with that?

explain.say: Now look at the right side. Both monkeys do the same job, but one now gets a grape, which capuchins love much more. The other still gets cucumber, and it saw everything. What do you think it does next?

explain.say: See the last line on the right? The monkey throws its cucumber back and shakes the cage, even though it was happy with cucumber a moment ago! Scientists call this inequity aversion, which means disliking unfair shares. So was the problem the cucumber, or the unfairness?

explain.say: Sarah Brosnan and Frans de Waal published this in 2003, and similar reactions have been seen in dogs, crows and chimpanzees, and in human toddlers. So a sense of fairness may be part of our nature, and rules and laws build on it. Brilliant! Challenge: notice one moment today when someone says "not fair", and ask what was unequal.

faq.a: Some seem to. Capuchin monkeys, chimpanzees, dogs and some birds react badly when a partner gets a better reward for the same task, which suggests a basic sense of fairness.
asks: Can animals tell what is fair?

faq.q: How did the monkey fairness experiment work?
faq.a: Capuchin monkeys traded a small rock with a researcher for food. Usually they got cucumber and were happy, which showed the task itself was fine.

faq.q: Why did the grape matter so much?
faq.a: Capuchins much prefer grapes to cucumber. Seeing a neighbour get a grape for the same job made the cucumber feel unfair, even though it was fine before.
asks: Tell me about sees a grape

faq.a: Inequity aversion means disliking unfair outcomes, especially getting less than someone else for the same effort. People and some animals will even give up a reward to protest unfairness.
asks: Why did the monkey throw the cucumber?

faq.a: Studies suggest even young children notice unfair shares, and babies around 15 months look longer at unequal sharing. Culture then shapes what each society thinks is fair.

facts: Sarah Brosnan and Frans de Waal published the capuchin cucumber-and-grape study in the journal Nature in 2003.
A 2011 study by Schmidt and Sommerville found 15-month-old babies looked longer when food was shared unequally, suggesting an early sense of fairness.
